name: Zâtî
bio: Zati was born in the province of Qarasi, where his father was a shoemaker, made his fortune in Constantinople, and was one of the poetic lights of the reigns of Bayezid II and Selim I.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poems.title: That Thy Form
poems.author: Zâtî
poems.text:
That thy form, O Beauty of His orchard who doth all pervade!
Is a cypress, wrought of light, that casteth on earth's face no shade.

Though the gazers on the loveliness of Joseph cut their hands,
Cleft in twain the fair moon's palm, when it thy day-bright face surveyed.

To the mart of the Hereafter, when a man hath passed, he gains
Through the money bright, thy love, which is of joy the stock-in-trade.

This, my hope, that yonder Cypress in the bowers of Paradise
Shelter Zâtî, and all true believers, 'neath his blissful shade.

poems.title: Ghazel: Glory of the Garth Etern, thy form in radiancy arrayed
poems.author: Zâtî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)
poems.text:
Glory of the Garth Etern, thy form in radiancy arrayed
Gleams a cypress wrought of light that casteth earthward naught of shade.

Though all they who looked on Joseph cut their hands, bewildered sore,
Cleft a-twain its palm what time the moon thy sun-bright face surveyed.

Far thy station, like the prayer-shaft's, beyond the nine-fold sphere;
Loftier than the lofty Empyrean is thy glorious grade.

There is none before or after equal unto thee in aught;
Seal of all the Prophet band, infinity thy dower is made.

He it is who gains, O Lord, when passed to the Hereafter's mart,
Who hath ta'en the coin of love of thee for all his stock-in-trade.

This my hope that mid the Paradisal bowers yon Cypress fair
Gather Zati with the faithful throng aneath the selfsame shade.

poems.title: Ghazel: A silver-bodied, sweetly shaven barber stripling fair
poems.author: Zâtî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)

poems.title: Ghazel: When we sight thy beauty, free will's bridle-rein doth pass away
poems.author: Zâtî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)
poems.text:
When we sight thy beauty, free will's bridle-rein doth pass away;
Champion-rider, grace we cry, the glaive of sdeign doth pass away.

By thy head, cast not thy lover down, bedecking thee so fair!
O my sweet, bethink thee, beauty's henna-stain doth pass away.

Be not vain a-thinking, 'All these birds of hearts I've made my prey.'
Prince of horsemen, grace's falcon lastwise fain doth pass away.

Kindness show to this ant Zati even as thou findest chance;
Solomon-renowned, the seal of beauty, vain doth pass away.

poems.title: Ghazel: What doth ail thee that thou meanest, Sphere? dost love a gadling free?
poems.author: Zâtî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)

poems.title: From the Shemʿ u Perwana
poems.author: Zâtî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)
poems.text:
What time Shemʿ and Perwana met again
The others passed and left alone these twain;
And when the King and Shemʿ were left alone
'Twas like the Sun conjoined with the Moon.
Their folk had piled the bed-gear nine-fold,
(The tale of what they did not is untold.)
A golden ladder thereagainst was laid,
Whereby the twain straightway upclomb the bed.
Soon as that Balm of Dole was mounted there
(As o'er the nine-fold sphere the faithful's prayer),
He stript her like unto a gentle dove
Naked, and held her to his breast with love.
He saw how fair that Lamb beseemed his breast,
He clasped her close and to his bosom prest.
And next he struck his teeth into the peach,
Delight he tasted, life his life did reach.
A harvest of the rose that bosom shone,
That night the bulbul the rose-harvest won.
From the King's hand the bird restraint takes flight,
His free will sinketh down and passeth quite.
That lover winneth to a silvery lawn,
And sees the foot-print of the heavenly fawn.
When reached the Monarch to that print his hand,
Thereunderneath a casket locked he fand,
The which he opened with a coral key,
And strewed with rubies all the drapery.
